cen0: Jaw Joint Problems (TMD): Symptoms and Exercises | İhsan Eren
cen1: Jaw pain, clicking and limited mouth opening: what causes jaw joint problems (TMD) and how do they ease? Daily tips and six jaw and neck exercises for home.
cen3: They cause pain in the jaw joint (temporomandibular joint), just in front of the ear, and in the chewing muscles, along with limited mouth opening and noises from the jaw. They affect about a third of adults and often get better with simple measures, exercise and physiotherapy.

cen7: Studies in the review looking at the effect of exercise and manual therapy
cen8: The jaw joint is where the lower jaw bone meets the skull, and it works whenever you talk, chew or yawn. Inside the joint there is a small disc that helps it move smoothly. The problem usually comes from overloading the chewing muscles, and sometimes from the disc moving out of place or from wear in the joint.
cen9: Teeth clenching and grinding during the day or at night, stress, keeping your mouth open for a long time, hard foods and blows to the jaw can all trigger symptoms.
cen10: Pain in front of the ear, in the cheek or at the temple
cen11: Pain that gets worse when you chew or talk for a long time
cen12: A clicking or crackling sound when you open and close your mouth
cen13: Limited mouth opening, or your jaw catching
cen14: Headache at the temple, a feeling of fullness in the ear
cen15: Most jaw joint problems are managed without surgery. In a review of 48 studies, manual therapy to the jaw or neck, on its own or combined with exercise, showed promising results; however, the researchers stress that the quality of the evidence is low and that better studies are needed.
cen16: Daily habits matter a lot: stick to soft foods for a while, don't chew gum, avoid big mouthfuls, support your jaw with your hand when you yawn, and try to notice whether you clench your teeth during the day. If stress makes your symptoms worse, take a look at the stress guide.
cen18: Noticing and changing the habits that strain your jaw is the first step of treatment.
cen19: Controlled mouth opening, exercises for the jaw and neck muscles, and posture exercises.
cen20: Techniques applied to the jaw joint, the chewing muscles and the neck can help reduce pain and increase how wide you can open your mouth.
cen22: If you clench or grind your teeth at night, your dentist can make one for you.
cen24: Applying gentle warmth to the chewing muscles can reduce tension.
cen25: Six exercises for the jaw and neck
cen26: Doing the movements slowly, without pain and in front of a mirror helps your jaw move without drifting to one side. Stop if the pain or catching gets worse.
cen28: Keep your lips closed and your teeth slightly apart, with the tip of your tongue resting on the roof of your mouth just behind your upper front teeth. Whenever you notice yourself clenching your teeth during the day, go back to this position.
cen29: Check it often throughout the day
cen30: Mouth opening with tongue on the palate
cen31: Place the tip of your tongue on the roof of your mouth, behind your upper front teeth. Keeping your tongue there, slowly open and close your mouth. Make sure your jaw moves in a straight line without drifting to the side; it can help to do this in front of a mirror.
cen34: Place your fist or two fingers under your chin. Try to open your mouth slightly while gently resisting with your hand; hold for 3–5 seconds, then relax. Using half your strength is enough, and it should not increase your pain.
cen37: Clench your teeth to find the chewing muscle in your cheek, then relax. Press gently on this muscle with your fingertips, making small circles. Doing it with a warm towel can be soothing.
cen38: My jaw makes noises. Do I need treatment?
cen39: A painless click is common and does not need treatment on its own. If the noise comes with pain, limited mouth opening or catching, it should be assessed.
cen40: Can clenching my teeth cause jaw pain?
cen41: Clenching your teeth during the day or at night tires the chewing muscles and can make pain worse. Try to notice during the day whether your teeth are touching; for clenching at night, your dentist may recommend a night guard (splint).
cen42: Do jaw joint problems go away?
cen43: For most people, symptoms ease over time with simple measures and exercises. If symptoms last a long time or keep getting worse, a dentist and a physiotherapist assess them together.
cen45: Very rarely. Surgery is considered for certain joint problems that do not respond to non-drug treatments; for most patients, the first choice is simple measures, exercise and physiotherapy.
cen46: Suddenly being unable to open your mouth, or your mouth getting stuck open and not closing
cen47: Swelling in the jaw or face, fever
cen48: Numbness or weakness in the face
cen49: Pain at the temple or problems with your vision, together with jaw pain that is new after the age of 50 and gets worse when you chew
